title: The Garden: date and context
short: Printed in 1681; usually linked to Marvell's time at Nun Appleton (c. 1650-52); a Latin companion poem, 'Hortus', also survives.
body: First printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681). Many critics associate it with Marvell's service as tutor to Mary Fairfax at Nun Appleton (c. 1650-52), though the date is uncertain. A Latin poem, 'Hortus', printed with it, treats similar material. The poem praises retirement over the active life, a theme with classical roots (Horace, Epode 2; Virgil, Georgics 2) and contemporary political resonance after the Civil War. 'Amaze' means bewilder, entangle as in a maze.

anchor: the Palm, the Oke, or Bayes
title: Palm, Oak, Bays
short: The three crowns of worldly achievement: palm for military victory, oak for civic service, bays (laurel) for poetry.
body: In Roman custom the palm signified victory, the oak wreath (corona civica) was awarded for saving a citizen's life, and the bay or laurel crowned poets and triumphant generals. Men exhaust themselves to win a garland from a single plant, whose narrow shade rebukes their toil, while the garden offers all plants' garlands of 'repose'. The Latin 'Hortus' makes the same contrast between public crowns and the garden's peace. The 'single Herb or Tree' of line 4 makes a rhetorical point: those who strive gain one plant, while the contemplative gains all.

title: verged
short: Bordered, edged: the shade of a single garland's foliage is narrow, a wry reproach to the toil spent winning it.
body: 'Verged' means bordered or limited. The shade cast by a wreath is tiny; the plant 'prudently' upbraids human striving. 'Close' in l. 7 means unite or join together. The stanza's argument is that the honours men pursue are small and grudging: the plant 'prudently' (wisely) upbraids the toil it rewards with so small a shade. In contrast, 'all Flow'rs and all Trees' freely weave garlands of repose for the retired man. The paradox of plenty in rest and scarcity in labour sets up the whole poem.

title: Quiet and Innocence
short: The speaker personifies Quiet and her sister Innocence, sought in vain in society but found among plants.
body: Quiet (otium) and innocence are the classical and Christian goods of retirement. The paradox that their 'sacred Plants' grow only among plants plays on the double sense of 'plant'. 'Rude' (l. 15) means uncultivated or barbarous; society compared with solitude is uncivilised. The speaker confesses that he 'Mistaken long' sought these virtues in 'busie Companies of Men', perhaps glancing at public life in the Civil War years. The stanza closes with an epigram that inverts the usual valuation of society and solitude, a classical topos (compare Cicero's report, De Officiis 3.1, that Scipio was never less alone than when alone).

title: delicious Solitude
short: Delightful, sensuously pleasing solitude; the word anticipates the sensuous fifth stanza.
body: 'Delicious' was a strong word, often used of sensual pleasure; applying it to solitude prepares for the garden's ripe fruits. The praise of solitude echoes a long tradition from Seneca to Montaigne's essay 'Of Solitude'. The word thus links the speaker's intellectual pleasure to physical delight. Critics differ on how far the poem's 'Solitude' is spiritual retirement and how far a witty, almost erotic, self-indulgence; Kermode reads it within the contemplative tradition, while others emphasise its sensuous play.

title: white and red vs green
short: The Petrarchan colours of female beauty (white skin, red lips) yield to green, the colour of the garden.
body: Petrarchan lovers praised the beloved's white and red complexion; Marvell declares the green of plants more 'am'rous'. The joke is that the speaker's love is for the trees themselves. Green, an important colour throughout the poem, culminates in the 'green Thought' of stanza 6. 'Am'rous' keeps its older sense of 'lovely, inspiring love'. The stanza is a joke against conventional love poetry, replacing the beloved with the vegetable world.

anchor: where s'eer you barkes I wound
title: carving names in bark
short: Lovers carve their mistresses' names in trees; the speaker would carve only the trees' own names.
body: Carving the beloved's name in bark was a pastoral convention (Virgil, Eclogue 10.53-54; Orlando in As You Like It). The speaker parodies it: he will wound the trees only with their own names. 'Fond' means foolish. 'S'eer' is 'soe'er', i.e. wheresoever. 'Hers' in line 22 means 'the mistress's beauties', which the trees' beauty far exceeds. The speaker reverses the convention: he wounds the bark only with the tree's own name.

title: Apollo and Daphne; Pan and Syrinx
short: Ovid's nymphs escape the gods by becoming laurel and reed; Marvell wittily claims the gods wanted the plants all along.
body: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 1, Daphne becomes a laurel to escape Apollo, and Syrinx becomes reeds to escape Pan, who makes his pipe from them. Marvell inverts the myths: the gods pursued the nymphs 'only' so they might become plants. The witty reinterpretation supports the stanza's claim that love's best retreat is the garden. 'Race' plays on the course of a pursuit and its end. The stanza converts erotic chase into a pursuit of vegetable peace: 'Love hither makes his best retreat' implies that desire, exhausted, finds rest among plants.

anchor: Ripe Apples drop about my head
title: the fruitful garden
short: A sensuous Eden in which fruit offers itself; the 'fall' on grass playfully recalls the Fall of Man.
body: The fruits press themselves upon the speaker, as in the golden age when the earth gave unbidden. The apple, the stumbling and the fall are a comic, innocent replay of Eden. 'Curious' means exquisite; 'Nectaren' is nectarine. Critics debate whether the stanza is innocent luxuriance or suggests temptation; Kermode reads it within a tradition of the garden as a place of contemplative pleasure.

title: from pleasure less
short: Ambiguous: the mind withdraws from lesser (sensual) pleasure, or is diminished by pleasure, into its own happiness.
body: The phrase allows several readings: (1) the mind, made less by pleasure, withdraws; (2) the mind withdraws from the lesser pleasure of the senses into its own greater happiness. Editors generally prefer the second, which marks the ascent from the senses to the intellect, a Neoplatonic movement. Empson discusses the ambiguity, seeing in such phrases the double meanings typical of Marvell's pastoral. 'Withdraws into its happiness' suggests both retreat and self-sufficiency.

title: the mind as Ocean
short: Popular belief held that every land creature had a counterpart in the sea; the mind likewise contains the images of all things.
body: Editors compare the 'vulgar error' that every land creature has its counterpart in the sea, which Sir Thomas Browne examined and doubted in Pseudodoxia Epidemica (1646). The mind contains ideas corresponding to everything in the world, a Platonic or Aristotelian notion. 'Streight' means straightaway. The mind then surpasses this mirroring by creating 'other Worlds, and other Seas'. The stanza's progression, from mirroring nature to creating new worlds, has been read as a Platonic ascent of the mind or as a celebration of poetic imagination.

title: a green Thought in a green Shade
short: The most famous line: the mind reduces all creation to a single green thought, whether annihilating or transcending it.
body: 'Annihilating' may mean reducing to nothing, or reducing to insignificance by comparison. 'Green' suggests fresh, innocent, immature, and the colour of the vegetable world. Empson discussed the line's balance between mind and nature; Kermode placed it in the tradition of contemplative ecstasy. Critics disagree whether the line shows mystical vision or witty paradox. The line's repetition of 'green' makes the thought and the shade almost identical, as if mind and nature merge. Smith surveys the range of readings, from Neoplatonic contemplation and Hermetic mysticism to witty parody of both.

title: the soul as bird
short: Casting off the body like a garment, the soul perches like a bird, preparing for its final flight to heaven.
body: The body as a 'Vest' (garment) cast aside is a Platonic image. The soul as a bird is an ancient emblem (cf. Plato's Phaedrus on the soul's wings). It 'whets' and 'combs' its wings and 'waves' the 'various Light' (many-coloured light), a Neoplatonic image of refracted divine light, before its 'longer flight' at death. 'Fountains sliding foot' means the base of a fountain where water slips away. The soul's preparation for 'longer flight' implies that this ecstasy is only a foretaste of death and heaven.

title: help meet
short: Adam was happiest alone: wittily reinterpreting Genesis 2:18, where God gives Adam a 'help meet' (Eve).
body: In Genesis 2:18, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him'. Marvell's playful misogyny claims Eden was perfect before Eve, so a mate was superfluous. 'Meet' means fitting. 'Two Paradises 'twere in one' suggests that solitude in Paradise would be a double paradise, which was beyond mortal lot. The tone is witty rather than doctrinal, but the stanza also recalls the Christian and classical ideal of the contemplative solitary.

title: the floral sundial
short: A sundial planted in flowers and herbs, with the sun moving through a 'fragrant Zodiack': time measured by nature.
body: Floral sundials laid out in herbs were features of seventeenth-century gardens. The 'skilful Gardner' may be the human gardener, or God, the divine artist. The bee 'computes its time', possibly punning on thyme. Time, measured by flowers, becomes sweet and wholesome, in contrast to the toil of the first stanza. The final stanza returns from the inner life to the visible garden and closes the poem on the sweetness of time well spent, recalling the opening contrast with 'uncessant Labours'.
